content.text: {"relation":"REFINED","consensus_summary":"Symbolic harlotry denotes covenant unfaithfulness, idolatry, or apostasy; in Revelation the precise referent is disputed, with imperial Rome or a corrupt world system prominent and unfaithful Jerusalem a recognized minority alternative.","book_summary":"The harlot is a covenant-breaker retaining the outward form of covenant, identified in Revelation specifically as unfaithful Jerusalem—the great city spiritually called Sodom, Egypt, and Babylon.","consensus_core_identification":"A covenantally unfaithful people, city, or system.","book_core_identification":"A false covenant community, specifically unfaithful Jerusalem in the Revelation context.","core_relation":"BOOK_NARROWS","extension_relation":"BOOK_SUBSET","boundary_disagreement":"The book restricts the image to covenant-breakers who retain covenant form and identifies Revelation’s great harlot as Jerusalem. The consensus permits a broader range of unfaithful peoples, cities, religious systems, and empires, and commonly identifies Revelation’s harlot with Rome or a transhistorical world system, though Jerusalem is a recognized alternative.","material_contradiction":"There is no contradiction with the settled general meaning of covenant unfaithfulness. There is a material referential disagreement with prominent Rome/world-system readings of Revelation 17, but not with the consensus as a whole because that specific referent is unsettled and Jerusalem is an established minority identification.","rationale":"The book preserves the consensus core—harlotry as covenant betrayal—but narrows both its conditions and application: the harlot has covenant form without substance, and Revelation’s woman is Jerusalem. This is a substantive boundary restriction rather than replacement of the central symbolic category, so REFINED is more appropriate than DIVERGENT or NOVEL.","citation_support":"PARTIAL","strongest_objection":"The printed citations establish that Ezekiel portrays covenantal Jerusalem as a harlot and that Revelation 11 calls the crucifixion site ‘the great city,’ while Revelation 17 calls the woman ‘that great city.’ They do not by themselves prove that both Revelation passages designate the same city or overcome Revelation 17:18’s description of a city reigning over the kings of the earth, which strongly supports the Rome identification for many interpreters.","confidence":"high"}
